specPoints.text: understand oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer and changes in oxidation number, and the application of these ideas to reactions of s- block and p- block elements
know that oxidising agents gain electrons and reducing agents lose electrons

primer.text: When electrons move, oxidation numbers move with them. This note links the electron transfer picture to the arithmetic of oxidation numbers, then names the two agents of every redox reaction: the oxidising agent that accepts electrons and falls, and the reducing agent that donates them and climbs.

lessons.title: Electron transfer through oxidation numbers
lessons.opening: Oxidation numbers turn electron transfer into arithmetic. This lesson follows nitrogen and bromine through the ammonia-bromine equation, watching one climb from -3 to 0 while the other falls from 0 to -1, and concludes who donated electrons to whom.
keyPoints: Oxidation and reduction can be demonstrated by changes in oxidation number during a reaction.
In 2NH3 + 3Br2 -> N2 + 6HBr, nitrogen rises from -3 in NH3 to 0 in N2.
A rising oxidation number means the species has been oxidised.
Bromine falls from 0 in Br2 to -1 in HBr, so bromine is reduced.
Nitrogen reduced bromine by donating electrons across the transfer.

low.restatement: Read the oxidation numbers before and after the reaction; the species whose number climbs is oxidised, the one that falls is reduced, and the electron flow runs from the climber to the faller.
low.analogy: Two bank accounts after a transfer: the balance that went up paid the money out (lost electrons), the balance that went down received it (gained electrons).
low.examPointer: Always write both states with signs - 'N goes -3 to 0' - before naming oxidised or reduced; the arithmetic earns the marks.

medium.restatement: Oxidation-number shifts quantify electron transfer: each unit rise equals one electron lost per atom, so nitrogen's 3-unit climb per atom pairs with bromine's 1-unit fall per atom, and the coefficients balance the ledger across the equation.
medium.analogy: A currency exchange where each nitrogen customer sells 3 coins and each bromine till takes exactly 1 - you need three bromine tills per nitrogen customer for the books to close.
medium.examPointer: Connect the ratio of oxidation-number changes to the equation's coefficients when asked why 3 Br2 appear per 2 NH3.

check.stem: In the ammonia-bromine reaction, what happens to nitrogen's oxidation number?

options.text: It rises from -3 to 0, so nitrogen is oxidised
options.explanation: The climb marks electron loss.

options.text: It falls from 0 to -3, so nitrogen is reduced
options.explanation: The direction is reversed.
Elemental N2 sits at 0.
Both states are misquoted.

check.stem: Bromine's oxidation number falls from 0 to -1. What has bromine done?

options.explanation: A falling number marks electron gain.
Electron loss raises the number.
Protons play no role in the redox bookkeeping.
The reduced species is the oxidising agent's client, not the donor.

check.stem: Which statement about the reaction 2NH3 + 3Br2 -> N2 + 6HBr is correct?

options.text: Nitrogen oxidised bromine by donating electrons
options.explanation: The climber is the donor.
Bromine's number fell, so it was reduced.
Both numbers shift clearly.
Hydrogen stays +1 throughout.

check.stem: Why do 3 Br2 molecules appear per 2 NH3 in the balanced equation?

options.text: Each N atom climbs 3 units while each Br atom falls 1, so the ledger needs three bromine atoms per nitrogen
options.explanation: The oxidation-number ledger fixes the stoichiometry.
Mass never sets stoichiometry.
The hydrogen count is not the ledger's driver.
Balancing follows the electron ledger exactly.

check.stem: Which pairing correctly links oxidation-number change to electron flow?

options.text: Number rises: electrons lost; number falls: electrons gained
options.explanation: The OIL RIG mapping in numeric form.
Gain would lower the number.
Loss raises the number.
Unchanged numbers mean no net transfer.

check.stem: State the oxidation number changes for nitrogen and bromine in the ammonia-bromine reaction.
check.modelAnswer: Nitrogen changes from -3 in NH3 to 0 in N2, and bromine changes from 0 in Br2 to -1 in HBr.

check.stem: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of oxidation number changes.
check.modelAnswer: Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number and reduction is a decrease in oxidation number.

check.stem: Explain why the species whose oxidation number rises must be the electron donor.
check.modelAnswer: Oxidation numbers count notional ionic charge, so a rising number means the atom holds more positive character, which can only come from losing negatively charged electrons - hence the climber donates.

check.stem: In the reaction, 2 N atoms each climb 3 units. How many electrons transfer in total per equation as written, and which species receives them?
check.modelAnswer: Two atoms times 3 units gives 6 electrons transferred, received by the 6 bromine atoms that each fall one unit.

lessons.title: The oxidising agent
lessons.opening: Every redox reaction employs two agents. This lesson profiles the oxidising agent: the species that oxidises something else by taking its electrons, dropping its own oxidation number in the process.
keyPoints: An oxidising agent oxidises another species by pulling its electrons away.
The oxidising agent itself gains those electrons and is therefore reduced.
Because it is reduced, the oxidising agent's oxidation number decreases.
The worked diagram shows the agent accepting electrons during the reaction.
Spotting the faller in an equation identifies the oxidising agent instantly.

low.restatement: The oxidising agent is the electron acceptor: it takes electrons from its partner, oxidises that partner, and falls in oxidation number itself.
low.analogy: A pawnbroker takes valuables (electrons) from clients (the species oxidised); the broker's drawer fills up while the client walks out lighter.
low.examPointer: Do not call the oxidising agent 'oxidised' - it IS reduced while it DOES the oxidising; the two roles are the classic exam trap.

medium.restatement: The agent's reduction is the mechanical cause of the partner's oxidation: accepting electrons pulls them off the partner, so the agent's oxidation number decreases by the electrons it accepts.
medium.analogy: A vacuum cleaner (the agent) reduces the dust pile by sucking (accepting) particles off the carpet (the partner), which loses them and is thereby cleaned out.
medium.examPointer: When asked to identify the agent, quote its oxidation-number fall with both states - assertion without arithmetic scores poorly.

check.stem: What does an oxidising agent do to another species?

options.text: Oxidises it by causing it to lose electrons
options.explanation: The agent strips electrons from its partner.
That describes a reducing agent.
Covalent sharing is not the agent's redox role.
Proton transfer belongs to acid-base chemistry.

check.stem: What happens to the oxidising agent itself?

options.explanation: Acceptance of electrons reduces the agent.
That is the partner's fate.
The agent's oxidation number clearly falls.
Agents are consumed stoichiometrically.

check.stem: How does the oxidising agent's oxidation number change?

options.explanation: Electron gain drives the number down.
That would mark the agent as oxidised.
Reduction always shifts the number.
No doubling rule exists.

check.stem: In Mg + Fe2+ -> Mg2+ + Fe, which species is the oxidising agent?

options.text: Fe2+, whose number falls from +2 to 0
options.explanation: The iron ion accepts magnesium's electrons.
The metal is oxidised - it is the donor.
Electrons are the currency, not an agent.
The reaction is textbook redox.

check.stem: Why must every redox reaction involve an oxidising agent?

options.text: Electrons lost by one species must be gained by another
options.explanation: The transfer needs both a donor and an acceptor.
Many redox reactions run without oxygen.

options.text: Agents are catalysts every reaction needs
options.explanation: Not every reaction is redox at all.

options.text: Charge would otherwise accumulate on the glassware
options.explanation: The conservation is chemical, not static electricity.

check.stem: Define the oxidising agent in one sentence.
check.modelAnswer: An oxidising agent oxidises another species by taking its electrons, and is itself reduced as those electrons arrive.

check.stem: State the direction of the oxidising agent's oxidation-number change and the reason.
check.modelAnswer: The oxidising agent's oxidation number decreases, because gaining electrons reduces it.

check.stem: Explain why the oxidising agent's own oxidation number falls while it oxidises its partner.
check.modelAnswer: The electrons the partner loses are accepted by the agent; added electrons lower the agent's notional ionic charge, so its number falls exactly as the partner's rises.

check.stem: In the chromium-dichromate style reaction, Cr2O7 2- falls from Cr at +6 to Cr3+ at +3. How many electrons does one dichromate ion accept, and what role does it play?
check.modelAnswer: Two chromium atoms each fall 3 units, so one dichromate ion accepts 6 electrons and acts as the oxidising agent.

lessons.title: The reducing agent and the worked pairing
lessons.opening: The reducing agent is the mirror twin. This lesson profiles the species that donates electrons, climbing as its partner falls, and works the four-reaction example where the bold species Fe2+ wins the agent title.
keyPoints: A reducing agent reduces another species by handing electrons over to it.
The reducing agent itself is oxidised, losing or donating electrons.
Because it is oxidised, the reducing agent's oxidation number increases.
A valid redox reaction needs both an oxidising and a reducing agent present.
Some substances can play either role, depending on their partner and the conditions.

low.restatement: The reducing agent hands electrons over: its own number climbs as it is oxidised, and its partner's number falls as it is reduced - both agents must appear for the reaction to be redox.
low.analogy: A donor at a blood bank: the donor (reducing agent) leaves with less (oxidised), the patient (partner) gains (reduced), and a transfusion needs one of each.
low.examPointer: In multiple-choice agent items, compute the bold species' oxidation numbers first - in the worked set, Fe2+ falling +2 to 0 wins the oxidising-agent title while Mg rises as the reducing agent.

medium.restatement: Donation drives the partner's reduction, so the reducing agent climbs in oxidation number; dual-role species such as hydrogen peroxide pick their direction from the partner's strength and the reaction conditions.
medium.analogy: A freelancer who can invoice or pay depending on the counterparty - the same species oxidises or reduces according to whom it meets.
medium.examPointer: For dual-role items, never assert a fixed role - say the role depends on the partner and the conditions to secure the mark.

check.stem: What does a reducing agent cause another species to do?

options.explanation: Donation fills the partner's empty slots.
That is what the oxidising agent causes.
State symbols never change by agency.
Dissociation is not a redox process.

check.stem: What happens to the reducing agent's oxidation number?

options.explanation: Electron loss drives the number up.
That marks reduction, not the agent's own fate.
Most reducing agents start bonded, not at zero.
Each reaction gives one clear direction.

check.stem: In the four-reaction worked set, why is Fe2+ in option 2 an oxidising agent?

options.text: It oxidises Mg(0) to Mg2+ while falling from +2 to Fe(0)
options.explanation: The bold species accepts magnesium's electrons.
Fe2+ receives the electrons.
No such change occurs in that equation.
The iron ends as elemental Fe.

check.stem: Which condition makes a redox reaction recognisable as such?

options.text: Both an oxidising and a reducing agent are present
options.explanation: One donor plus one acceptor defines the redox pair.
Colour changes mark many non-redox processes.
Gas release is common in acid-base work too.
Exothermicity is not the redox criterion.

check.stem: Why might hydrogen peroxide act sometimes as oxidiser and sometimes as reducer?

options.text: Its role depends on the partner species and the reaction conditions
options.explanation: Dual-role agents switch direction according to context.

options.text: It has no fixed oxidation state at all
options.explanation: Its oxygen sits at -1, a fixed value.
Decomposition is itself a redox process.
The dual behaviour is intrinsic chemistry.

check.stem: Define the reducing agent in one sentence.
check.modelAnswer: A reducing agent reduces another species by handing electrons over to it, and is itself oxidised as those electrons leave.

check.stem: State the direction of the reducing agent's oxidation-number change.
check.modelAnswer: The reducing agent's oxidation number increases, because losing electrons oxidises it.

check.stem: Explain why a redox reaction cannot contain only a reducing agent.
check.modelAnswer: Electrons donated must be accepted somewhere; with no oxidising agent present, the donated electrons would have no recipient and the charge ledger could not balance.

check.stem: In Mg + Fe2+ -> Mg2+ + Fe, magnesium rises 0 to +2 and iron falls +2 to 0. How many electrons transfer per equation, and which agent donated them?
check.modelAnswer: Two electrons transfer per equation, donated by the reducing agent magnesium.

glossary.definition: The species that accepts electrons from its partner, oxidising the partner while being reduced itself.
The species that donates electrons to its partner, reducing the partner while being oxidised itself.
The movement of electrons from donor to acceptor that underlies every redox reaction.
